rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: Jumping spiders have eight simple eyes, and you very likely have eight as well. If you are a bold jumping spider, your two big front eyes follow a moving target precisely only while the smaller eyes beside them guide them. Nobody has measured what each of your eyes does in most species, so for you the full division of work is unknown.
rows.note: Left out Lyssomanes (vestigial rear median eyes, R5) and the Menemerus and Habronattus findings (R1, R3) because they belong to other genera and the row would grow past three sentences.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Nobody has measured how sharply most of you see, only how closely your light-sensing cells sit. If you are a bold jumping spider, the cells in the sharpest zone of your side eyes sit about half a degree apart. In the big front eyes of Phidippus johnsoni, a relative, they sit about 9 minutes of arc apart, which is much less than a degree.
rows.note: Removed the 60 minutes per degree figure, which no record states. Left out R3 because its quote gives only a visual angle, and R5 to avoid decimals.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: If you are a bold jumping spider, each of the eyes beside your two big front eyes sees an area about 70 degrees wide and about 100 degrees tall, so it reaches farther up and down than side to side. For other jumping spiders, nobody has measured these fields. Nobody has measured how far all your eyes together see around you, or how much the fields of your two side eyes overlap.
rows.note: Left out R8 (about 25 degrees of overlap, Blest 1981): it is a genus-level discussion statement and the row's binocular trait is unknown. Also left out the Phidippus johnsoni and Menemerus carried values, since they don't fit one plain sentence.

rows.title: Eye movement
rows.text: In an eyetracker study of jumping spiders, the retinas inside the two big front eyes moved, and the spiders spent more time looking at still or slowly moving images. If you are a bold jumping spider, your front eyes need guidance from the pair of eyes beside them to find and follow a moving object, but they scan a still shape without that guidance. Nobody has measured the eye movements of most other jumping spiders, so how your own retinas move is unknown.
rows.note: Left out the fovea: R5's quote does not state the receptor density figure, and R3 covers only Lyssomanes. R2 (Marpissa marina priming) left out for length.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: In every jumping spider measured, the big front eyes have cells that sense ultraviolet and cells that sense green. A regal jumping spider has three kinds of color-sensing cell, and Habronattus pyrrithrix gets a third color channel, for red, only in a small patch at the center of the retina, while Plexippus validus has just two kinds. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have unless you are one of those species.
rows.note: Left out the color-discrimination behavior (R12, Evarcha falcata) and wavelength figures because they add no comparison here. R8 gives three cell types in the regal jumping spider but does not say which kinds, so the row does not say.

rows.title: Movement
rows.text: If you are a bold jumping spider, your front eyes scan in a different pattern depending on whether moving dots move like a living animal and whether the dots form a shape. If you are a gray wall jumping spider, small, fast, thin stripes weaken the response of your front eyes' retinas. Nobody has measured how most other jumping spiders see movement, and in the magnolia green jumping spider the side-eye retina is less refined for motion than in the other jumping spiders studied.
rows.note: Left out the 120 to 1200 degrees/s turning speeds (R14) and the 16 degrees/s figure (R15) because those records name only the family, not a species.

rows.title: Vibration and sound
rows.text: A low tone played from more than 3 meters away makes a bold jumping spider freeze, and male brilliant jumping spiders court with vibrations whose rate affects how well they mate. Those are two of the few jumping spiders measured for sound or vibration. Nobody has measured what you hear or feel through your legs if you are any other jumping spider.
rows.note: Left out R1 (recorded under Corythalia canosa, not matched to the listed name), R3 and R5 to stay within three sentences.
